1.pericope_label: Bezaleel, Aholiab and every wise hearted man begin the work; Moses calls them, and every one whose heart stirred him up comes to do it

schools.summary: Calvin defends the repetition as allowing an actual comparison of work with pattern, since nothing human was to enter the structure and no workman might give scope to his own inventions, and argues from the Spirit-given skill against those who cite such passages for free will; Gill supposes a particular workshop where the craftsmen were ranged by trade, and holds that a call from the Lord and from the church is needed as well as fitness.
Henry reads the prompt beginning as a lesson that talents are to be traded with rather than laid up, and insists that even the qualified must wait for a regular call.

Clarke argues that the first verse belongs to the preceding chapter and reads its opening verb as a future by the conversive force of the Hebrew conjunction; Wesley reproduces Henry’s judgment on the call and concludes that ability and willingness together qualify a man for the work.

Ellicott takes the verse as introductory to a section reaching to the end of the thirty-ninth chapter, grants that it is little more than a repetition of the earlier chapters, and finds the exactness deliberate, teaching that obedience must be complete down to the smallest point; he also lists the materials handed over at the summons.

debates: Where the verse belongs and how the section should be read. Clarke would attach it to the preceding chapter and change the tense of its verb to make the sense run; Ellicott keeps it here as the introduction to the whole execution narrative.

3.pericope_label: And they received of Moses all the offering which the children of Israel had brought for the work of the service of the sanctuary; and they brought yet unto him free offerings every morning

schools.summary: Gill follows the materials into the workshop, distributed as each man’s task required, and notes that Moses gave out faithfully all he received and kept back nothing for himself; Calvin finds prudence in the distribution, diligence in beginning before the materials sufficed, and integrity in stopping the offerings, and contrasts the people’s liberality out of small means with the idolatry that soon followed, concluding that the zeal came from the Spirit and that all our best feelings vanish without the gift of steadfastness.

Ellicott follows the second clause, a liberality that continued morning after morning until the workmen had more than enough, and sets beside it the giving under David and at the rearing of the second temple; Keil and Delitzsch paraphrase the workmen’s report, note the comparative force of the preposition, and describe the proclamation that stopped further giving.

4.pericope_label: The wise men leave their work to tell Moses the people bring more than enough; he has it proclaimed through the camp that none bring more, and the stuff is sufficient and too much

schools.summary: Gill identifies the men who came as the craftsmen employed on the several parts, has one speak for the rest, and keeps to the plain sense that what had already been brought in sufficed for everything ordered.

Clarke argues from the proclamation to the character of Moses, who could have encouraged the flow and enriched himself and did not, and generalises that a people whose hearts are in the worship of God will provide for it cheerfully.

Keil and Delitzsch attend to the wording of the proclamation and to the word for sufficiency with its literal remainder, and read the liberality as the people proving their willingness to uphold the covenant; Ellicott infers from the verb “make” that the surplus was chiefly things produced by labour, so that the humblest contributors were the most zealous, and asks when Christian liberality will need restraining.

outliers: Clarke leaves the episode to argue that the national clergy of his own country should be supported by some method other than tithes.

8.pericope_label: Every wise hearted man among them made ten curtains of fine twined linen, blue, purple and scarlet, with cherubims of cunning work, all of one size

schools.summary: Gill marks the change of subject and refers the reader to his comments on the earlier chapter, notes that each man did the part he was fittest for and that the curtains which were properly the tabernacle came first, and raises the question whom the repeated singular verb refers to.

Henry reads the curtained house as a type of the church in this world, standing on the earth but not founded in it, mean and mutable and militant like the tents of shepherds and soldiers, yet embroidered as the church is adorned with the gifts of the Spirit, and coupled into one as believers are.

Clarke takes the word rendered cherubim to mean figures of any kind, woven, embroidered, carved or engraved, and reports that able critics have contended for that sense, while granting that elsewhere it seems restricted to one well-known figure.

Keil and Delitzsch answer that the verbs are third person singular with an indefinite subject, like the German man or the French on, and set out the structure of the section against the corresponding parts of the earlier instructions.

debates: Whom the repeated singular verb refers to. Gill offers Moses, Bezaleel or each craftsman severally; Keil and Delitzsch settle it grammatically, the singular being impersonal with an indefinite subject.
What the cherubim were. Clarke argues the word means figures of any kind produced by loom, needle or graving tool, while allowing that in some places it denotes a particular figure then well known.

14.pericope_label: And he made curtains of goats’ hair for the tent over the tabernacle

schools.summary: Henry reads the hair-cloth curtains and the skins above them as the shelter and special protection the church enjoys, a shadow from the heat and a covert from storm that does not let the rain in however long the dropping, and the boards and bars beneath as its strength and stability, since it is the union of those who are the church’s stays that holds the frame together.

30.pericope_label: Two sockets under every board; and for the sides of the tabernacle westward he made six boards

schools.summary: Clarke does no more than refer the reader back to his comment on the making of the bars.

Ellicott holds that “under every board two sockets” is the true meaning but cannot be got from the present text, the Hebrew phrase having accidentally dropped out in one of the two places where the parallel passage repeats it; he also corrects “the sides westward” to the back of the tabernacle westward.

35.pericope_label: And he made a veil of blue, and purple, and scarlet, and fine twined linen: with cherubims made he it of cunning work

schools.summary: Henry gives the inner veil a double sense, the darkness and distance of the older dispensation against a New Testament that shows God’s glory more clearly, and the darkness and distance of the present state against heaven; and reads the outer curtain as the place where a people forbidden to enter still assembled, since we must get as near to God as we can.
Wesley takes over the first of those two senses almost word for word and stops there; Clarke adds only a pointer back to his note on the veil in the earlier chapter.

37.pericope_label: And he made a hanging for the tabernacle door, and the five pillars of it with their hooks

schools.summary: Clarke refers the reader back to the earlier chapter and glosses the hooks as capitals, observes that this chapter and those following are in general a repetition of what was given in detail from the twenty-fifth chapter on, and explains why the repetition was necessary: the command had been recorded, and without an account of the execution it could not be known that the work was done according to the pattern. He also explains an apparent discrepancy in his own chapter dates, the years of the world and before Christ beginning at Tisri while the years of the exodus are dated from Abib.

outliers: Clarke closes with a note reconciling two of his own dating scales rather than with a comment on the verse.
